newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Southeast spot power stable, more nukes down.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Southeast spot power stable, more nukes down.

text.p: Trading of spot wholesale electricity in the southeastern U.S. was relatively stable Friday despite today's news of Duke Power Co idling two more nuclear units at its Oconee complex in Seneca, S.C.
"I have not seen a big jump. There's plenty of excess (power) from ECAR (East Central Area Reliability Coordination Agreement)," said a Southeast trader.

Duke said Friday it was shutting Oconee units 1 and 3, prompted by a steam pipe rupture at unit 2, which injured seven workers on Sept 24. The utility planned to keep units 1 and 2 down until mid-November, and unit 3 mid-December.
All three Oconee units are rated at 846 megawatt (MW).
Most participants said mild weather and scheduled return of Duke's 1,129 MW Catawba nuclear unit 1 would offset the loss of the Oconee units.
Duke, which owns 25 percent interests in Catawba 1, expected the Clover, S.C., unit to resume full output some time next week following a scheduled refueling and maintenance program.
"The weather's so mild, and they (Duke) have Catawba coming back," a Houston trader said.

In the Southeastern Electric Reliability Council (SERC), peak, firm electricity during heavy load hours for the weekend for delivery into the northern part of Tennessee Valley Authority's (TVA) system was quoted near $14.00 a megawatt hour (MWh) for the weekend and $14.50 for Monday, compared with Thursday's $16.00-$17.00 range.
At the Georgia-Florida border, firm, peak electricity was valued at $21.00-$21.50 a MWh for this weekend and $22.00-$22.75 for Monday, compared with $21.00-$22.00 on Thursday.
TVA was heard offering peak, non-firm electricity for Saturday at $16.50; Sunday $15.50; and Monday $17.50, compared with Thursday offer for Friday at $17.50.
